decks.name: Basic Principles of Pharmacology
decks.description: Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, drug kinetics, teratogens, and clinical trials

decks.name: Autonomic Pharmacology
decks.description: Cholinergic and adrenergic agonists and antagonists, neuromuscular blockers, and related toxicity

decks.name: Cardiovascular Pharmacology
decks.description: Antihypertensives, antianginals, heart failure drugs, antiarrhythmics, diuretics, and lipid-lowering agents

decks.name: Autacoids and Respiratory Pharmacology
decks.description: Serotonin, histamine, prostaglandins, asthma drugs, and respiratory agents

decks.name: CNS Pharmacology
decks.description: Neurotransmitters, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, Parkinson drugs, sedatives, anesthetics, opioids, and drugs of abuse

decks.name: Hematology, NSAIDs, DMARDs and Gout
decks.description: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, fibrinolytics, iron, growth factors, NSAIDs, DMARDs, and gout drugs

decks.name: Endocrine Pharmacology
decks.description: Pituitary, reproductive hormones, thyroid, adrenal, diabetes, calcium and bone drugs

decks.name: Antibiotics, Antimycobacterials and Antifungals
decks.description: Antibacterial agents, antituberculosis and antileprosy drugs, and antifungals

decks.name: Antivirals, Antiparasitics and Antiseptics
decks.description: Antiviral and antiretroviral drugs, antimalarials, antiprotozoals, anthelmintics, and STI treatments

decks.name: Cancer Chemotherapy
decks.description: Chemotherapeutic agents, toxicities, rescue agents, regimens, and targeted therapies

decks.name: Gastrointestinal Pharmacology
decks.description: Antacids, acid suppressants, laxatives, antiemetics, antidiarrheals, IBS, IBD, and hepatobiliary agents

decks.name: Immunopharmacology
decks.description: Immunosuppressants, immune potentiators, and monoclonal antibodies

decks.name: Toxicology
decks.description: Antidotes, chelating agents, and heavy metal and organic toxin syndromes

cards.front: Any substance that changes biologic function through its chemical actions
Rank drug-receptor bonds from strongest to weakest.
cards.back: Covalent > Electrostatic > Hydrophobic. The stronger the bond, the more irreversible the binding.

cards.front: The study of how drugs act on the body (mechanisms of action, receptor interactions, effects)
The study of how the body acts on a drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion)
Specific molecules in a biologic system with which drugs interact to produce changes
cards.back: Receptors (the recognition site is the specific binding region)

cards.front: A molecule or system that translates the drug-receptor interaction into a change in cellular activity
Maximum effect an agonist can produce regardless of dose
cards.back: Emax (maximal efficacy). Higher efficacy means greater intrinsic activity.

cards.front: Amount of drug required to produce a given effect
Efficacy is determined mainly by what?
cards.back: The nature of the receptor and its associated effector system

cards.front: Potency is determined mainly by what?
cards.back: The affinity of the receptor for the drug

cards.front: Graph of dose or drug concentration versus fraction of the population that responds at each dose
Graph of dose or drug concentration versus response
Formula for therapeutic index
cards.back: Therapeutic index = TD50 / ED50. A larger value means a wider safety margin.

cards.front: Components of a graded dose-response curve
Components of a quantal dose-response curve
cards.back: ED50 (median effective dose), TD50 (median toxic dose), LD50 (median lethal dose)

cards.front: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (mnemonic: Amp, Ang sikip if Car Farin, PaPaLit Daw Tayo ng Van)
cards.back: Amphotericin B, Aminoglycosides, Carbamazepine, Warfarin, Phenobarbital, Phenytoin, Lithium, Digoxin, Theophylline, Vancomycin

cards.front: Narrow therapeutic index drugs (mnemonic: Warning! These Drugs Are Lethal)
cards.back: Warfarin, Theophylline, Digoxin, Antiepileptic drugs, Lithium

cards.front: A drug capable of fully activating the effector system when it binds to the receptor
In the presence of a full agonist, this drug type acts as an antagonist.
A drug that blocks or dampens the response to an agonist
Example of a physiologic antagonist
cards.back: Histamine and epinephrine. They bind to different receptors that produce opposite effects.

cards.front: Antagonist that interacts directly with the drug to remove it or prevent it from reaching its target
cards.back: Chemical antagonist (directly binds the drug molecule)

cards.front: Antagonist that binds the same receptor as the agonist
Antagonist that competes with the agonist for the primary binding site. Effect on the dose-response curve?
cards.back: Competitive (reversible) antagonist. Rightward shift of the curve with unchanged Emax (surmountable with more agonist).

cards.front: Antagonist that binds irreversibly (usually covalent) to the receptor. Effect on the dose-response curve?
cards.back: Non-competitive (irreversible) antagonist. Downward shift of Emax.

cards.front: Enzyme kinetics: increased Km, no change in Vmax
Enzyme kinetics: no change in Km, decreased Vmax
Properties of drugs that favor absorption (mnemonic LUNA)
Fraction of an administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation
Steady state is reached after how many half-lives?
Route with no absorption phase (100% bioavailability)
In an acidic environment, what happens to absorption and excretion of a weak acid?
cards.back: Absorption increases, excretion decreases (the weak acid stays un-ionized).

cards.front: In an acidic environment, what happens to absorption and excretion of a weak base?
cards.back: Absorption decreases, excretion increases (the weak base becomes ionized and trapped).

cards.front: Three major factors affecting absorption
cards.back: 1. Route of administration 2. Blood flow 3. Concentration

cards.front: Plasma protein to which basic drugs bind
Plasma protein to which acidic drugs bind
Key phase I reactions
Key phase II reactions
CYP inducers (mnemonic: PRC! G, aral na!)
cards.back: Phenytoin, Rifampicin, Carbamazepine, Chronic alcohol, Griseofulvin (also barbiturates and St. John's wort)

cards.front: CYP inhibitors (mnemonic: SICKFACES.COM)
cards.back: Sodium valproate, Isoniazid, Cimetidine, Ketoconazole, Fluconazole, Amiodarone, Alcohol (acute), Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin, Sulfonamides, Ciprofloxacin, Omeprazole, Metronidazole

cards.front: A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time and enzymes are not saturated
A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time because of enzyme saturation
Maintenance dose formula
Volume of distribution formula
cards.back: Vd = Amount of drug in the body / Plasma drug concentration

cards.front: Loading dose formula
cards.back: Loading dose = (Vd x desired plasma concentration) / Bioavailability

cards.front: Drugs with zero-order elimination kinetics (mnemonic: WHAT PET)
cards.back: Warfarin, Heparin, Aspirin, Tolbutamide, Phenytoin, Ethanol, Theophylline. Most important: PEA (Phenytoin, Ethanol, Aspirin).

cards.front: Most important pharmacokinetic parameter in defining a rational steady-state dosage regimen
Clearance formula
cards.back: CL = Rate of elimination / Plasma concentration

cards.front: Toxin associated with moldy peanuts or rice and hepatocellular carcinoma
Toxin in PVC pipe factories associated with liver angiosarcoma
Teratogen causing phocomelia (seal limbs)
Teratogen causing tooth discoloration
Teratogen causing aplasia cutis congenita
Teratogen causing Ebstein anomaly
Teratogen causing vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma
Warfarin teratogenicity per trimester
cards.back: 1st: chondrodysplasia punctata (nasal hypoplasia). 2nd: CNS malformations. 3rd: bleeding diatheses.

cards.front: Legacy FDA pregnancy category: no human studies and safe in animals, or safe in humans but unsafe in animals
Legacy FDA pregnancy category: unsafe in humans and animals, but benefits may outweigh risks. Examples?
cards.back: Category D. Examples: ACE inhibitors, some anticonvulsants.

cards.front: Clinical trial phase that mainly tests efficacy in a small population with the disease
Clinical trial phase that mainly tests safety in healthy volunteers
Post-marketing surveillance corresponds to which clinical trial phase?
Cholinergic toxicity mnemonic: DUMBELLS
cards.back: Diarrhea/diaphoresis, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia (or tachycardia if nicotinic), Emesis, Lacrimation, Lethargy, Salivation

cards.front: Anticholinergic toxicity mnemonic (Alice in Wonderland)
cards.back: Hot as a hare (hyperthermia), Dry as a bone (decreased secretions), Red as a beet (cutaneous vasodilation), Blind as a bat (cycloplegia, mydriasis), Mad as a hatter (CNS toxicity)

cards.front: Muscarinic agonist causing detrusor contraction, used for urinary retention
Drugs that relax the detrusor and are used for urinary incontinence
cards.back: Muscarinic antagonists (oxybutynin) and the beta-3 agonist mirabegron

cards.front: Drug class that relaxes the bladder neck and prostate, used for BPH
Drug used in postoperative and diabetic bladder neuropathy
Drug inhibiting the choline transporter, blocking acetylcholine synthesis
Drug inhibiting vesicular storage of acetylcholine
Drug inhibiting acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Drug inhibiting vesicular storage of catecholamines
Drugs inhibiting degradation of acetylcholine into choline and acetate
Mechanism of action of succinylcholine
Enzyme that degrades succinylcholine
Agent used in the Tensilon test for myasthenia gravis
Drug of choice for myasthenia gravis. Does it cross the BBB?
cards.back: Pyridostigmine (preferred over neostigmine). Quaternary amines do not cross the BBB.

cards.front: Drugs that can worsen myasthenia gravis
cards.back: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers and aminoglycosides (also fluoroquinolones and macrolides)

cards.front: Muscarinic agonist that triggers lacrimal and salivary secretion, used in glaucoma and xerostomia (Sjogren)
Direct cholinergic used in the bronchial challenge test for asthma
Cholinergic agonists susceptible to degradation by AChE
Cholinergic agonists with nicotinic action
Treatment for muscarinic toxicity from agonist overdose or Amanita muscaria mushrooms
Treatment of organophosphate poisoning
cards.back: Pralidoxime to regenerate AChE, and atropine to manage muscarinic symptoms

cards.front: Treatment for atropine poisoning. Why does it work centrally?
cards.back: Physostigmine, a tertiary amine that crosses the BBB

cards.front: Alzheimer disease treatment
cards.back: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine. NMDA antagonist: memantine.

cards.front: Prototype muscarinic antagonist
Antimuscarinic that blocks all muscarinic receptors and is used for motion sickness
Muscarinic blockers used for asthma and COPD
cards.back: Ipratropium and tiotropium (tiotropium is more selective for M3 and longer acting)

cards.front: Competitive Nn (ganglionic) blocker, obsolete antihypertensive causing postural hypotension
Epinephrine dose: ACLS vs anaphylaxis
cards.back: ACLS: 1 mg of 1:10,000 IV. Anaphylaxis: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM.

cards.front: Alpha-1 selective agonist that can activate beta receptors at very high concentrations
Treatment for alpha-1 agonist overdose
Alpha-2 agonist known to cause rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal
Drug that inhibits catecholamine synthesis by inhibiting tyrosine hydroxylase
Alpha agonist decongestants (-ZOLINEs) that can cause rebound nasal congestion
Nonselective beta-1, beta-2, beta-3 agonist. Adverse effects?
Indirect-acting sympathomimetics used in ADHD
Dietary substance in cured meats that can cause hypertensive crisis with MAO inhibitors
Beta-1 agonist used for cardiogenic shock
Side effects of beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline, formoterol)
General adverse effects of alpha blockers
cards.back: Orthostatic hypotension and reflex tachycardia (can trigger arrhythmias and MI)

cards.front: Irreversible alpha blocker used for pheochromocytoma
Reversible nonselective alpha blocker
Most selective alpha-1A blocker for prostatic smooth muscle
Beta blockers with combined alpha and beta blockade
Beta blockers can cause severe hypotension or bradycardia when combined with which drug class?
Cardioselective (beta-1) blockers (mnemonic: Celip 1st! B selective about your MAN, BABE)
cards.back: Celiprolol, Metoprolol, Atenolol, Nebivolol, Betaxolol, Acebutolol, Bisoprolol, Esmolol

cards.front: Beta blocker lacking local anesthetic effect, used as eye drops
Shortest and longest acting beta blockers
Beta blocker that increases nitric oxide production
Drug of choice for beta blocker toxicity
Prostaglandin analogues used in glaucoma. Mechanism?
cards.back: Latanoprost, bimatoprost. They increase aqueous humor outflow.

cards.front: Glaucoma drugs that decrease aqueous humor production
cards.back: Beta antagonists, alpha-2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (osmotic agents lower intraocular pressure acutely)

cards.front: First-line antihypertensives
cards.back: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics

cards.front: Side effects of ACE inhibitors (-PRILs)
Contraindications of ACE inhibitors
cards.back: Pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis

cards.front: Examples of ARBs (-SARTANs)
ARB with added PPAR-gamma agonist activity, beneficial in insulin resistance
Mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics
cards.back: Inhibit the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

cards.front: Side effects of thiazides (mnemonic HYPER-GLUC)
cards.back: HyperGlycemia, HyperLipidemia, HyperUricemia, HyperCalcemia. Also hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and dilutional hyponatremia.

cards.front: Mechanism of action of loop diuretics
cards.back: Inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

cards.front: Loop diuretic that is not a sulfonamide
Side effects of loop diuretics (mnemonic OH DANG)
cards.back: Ototoxicity, Hypokalemia, Dehydration, Allergy to sulfa, Nephritis (interstitial), Gout

cards.front: CCBs block which type of calcium channel?
Two types of CCBs and examples
cards.back: Dihydropyridines (-DIPINEs): nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, nicardipine. Non-dihydropyridines: verapamil and diltiazem.

cards.front: Side effects of CCBs
cards.back: Constipation (especially verapamil), pretibial edema (common with DHPs), gingival hyperplasia (amlodipine, verapamil)

cards.front: Antihypertensive that can cause hemolytic anemia and is used in pregnancy
Antihypertensive class with first-dose syncope and orthostatic hypotension
Can beta blockers be given in acute or chronic heart failure?
cards.back: Chronic HF only. Do not start in acute decompensated HF.

cards.front: Drug that causes rebound hypertension or hypertensive urgency if stopped abruptly
Hydralazine: mechanism and uses
cards.back: Alters intracellular Ca2+ metabolism causing arteriolar vasodilation. Used in pre-eclampsia and hypertension.

cards.front: Side effects of hydralazine
cards.back: Drug-induced lupus, reflex tachycardia, headache. Severe psychiatric depression and suicidal ideation have been reported.

cards.front: Mechanism of action of minoxidil and diazoxide
cards.back: Open K+ channels in vascular smooth muscle

cards.front: Mechanism of action of aliskiren
Treatment of Prinzmetal (variant) angina
cards.back: CCBs and nitrates (diltiazem is a drug of choice)

cards.front: D1 receptor agonist used to increase renal blood flow
First-line therapy for stable angina
Nitrates combined with this drug class cause dangerous hypotension
Treatment of methemoglobinemia
Alternating tolerance and loss of tolerance due to occupational nitrate exposure
Drugs for hypertension in pregnancy (mnemonic Hi, MeLaNi)
Components of a cyanide antidote kit
cards.back: Inhaled amyl nitrite, IV sodium nitrite, IV sodium thiosulfate

cards.front: Ranolazine: mechanism, side effect, use
cards.back: Reduces late Na+ current into myocardial cells. Causes QT prolongation. Used for chronic angina prophylaxis.

cards.front: Antianginal that shifts metabolism from fatty acid oxidation to glucose oxidation
Mechanism of action of ivabradine
cards.back: Selectively inhibits If (funny) channels in the SA node, lowering heart rate

cards.front: Nitrate with longer half-life and no first-pass effect
Cornerstone drugs in heart failure with reduced EF
cards.back: ACE inhibitor/ARB (or ARNI), beta blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors

cards.front: Key beta blockers for heart failure
cards.back: Bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (reduce progression of chronic HF)

cards.front: Enzyme that degrades atrial and brain natriuretic peptide. Which drug inhibits it?
Side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
cards.back: Genital mycotic infections, UTI, volume depletion and dizziness, euglycemic ketoacidosis, Fournier gangrene

cards.front: Most common ECG finding in digoxin toxicity
Mechanism of each Vaughan Williams class (mnemonic NaBaKlaCa)
cards.back: Class 1: Na channel blockers. Class 2: beta blockers. Class 3: K channel blockers. Class 4: Ca channel blockers.

cards.front: Effect of Class 1 antiarrhythmics on action potential duration
Class 1A antiarrhythmic with cinchonism
Class 1B antiarrhythmic with agranulocytosis
Class 1B antiarrhythmic with least cardiotoxicity and significant first-pass effect
Antiarrhythmic class contraindicated post-MI
Most efficacious antiarrhythmic drug
Side effects of amiodarone
cards.back: Corneal microdeposits, blue-gray skin discoloration, thyroid dysfunction (hyper or hypo), paresthesia, tremor, pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity

cards.front: Antiarrhythmic classes that can cause torsades de pointes
Drug of choice for torsades de pointes
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate (hypotension and bradycardia if given too fast IV)

cards.front: Drug of choice for paroxysmal or narrow-complex SVT. Side effect?
cards.back: Adenosine. Sense of impending doom; half-life about 15 seconds.

cards.front: Common side effect of spironolactone
Drug used in central diabetes insipidus and von Willebrand disease
Diuretic causing normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis
Potassium-sparing diuretics that block ENaC
V1 and V2 receptor antagonists used in SIADH
Mechanism of statins
Common adverse effects of statins
Drug of choice for hypertriglyceridemia
Fibrates plus resins increase risk of what?
Statins plus resins cause what interaction?
Statins plus fibrates increase risk of what?
Examples of high-intensity statin therapy
Agent best at increasing HDL. Notable side effects?
Niacin-induced flushing is reduced by which drug?
Side effects of bile acid binding resins
cards.back: Steatorrhea and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin K)

cards.front: Mechanism of fibrates
Drug classes that control rate in atrial arrhythmias
cards.back: Class II (beta blockers such as metoprolol, propranolol) and Class IV (non-dihydropyridine CCBs: verapamil, diltiazem)

cards.front: Drug classes that control rhythm in atrial arrhythmias
cards.back: Class I (flecainide, propafenone) and Class III (amiodarone, sotalol)

cards.front: Antiarrhythmic with the most mechanisms of action
cards.back: Amiodarone (Class I, II, III, and IV effects)

cards.front: Endogenous molecules with powerful pharmacologic effects that do not fall into the traditional autonomic groups
cards.back: Autacoids. Histamine and serotonin are the most important amine autacoids.

cards.front: 5-HT1B/1D agonists, drug of choice for acute migraine. Side effect?
cards.back: Triptans (sumatriptan, naratriptan). Chest pain or tightness.

cards.front: Ergot compounds act on which receptor?
Ergot compound selective for uterine muscle
5-HT3 antagonists: use and side effects
cards.back: -SETRONs. Chemotherapy-induced and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Constipation and QT prolongation.

cards.front: 5-HT4 partial agonist for IBS with constipation
Cause of ergotism (St. Anthony's fire)
cards.back: Ergot alkaloids: vasospasm leading to gangrene plus hallucinations

cards.front: Classic demonstration of the histamine effect
cards.back: Triple response of Lewis: wheal, flush, and flare

cards.front: Receptor responsible for allergic reactions
Major side effect of first-generation H1 blockers
Second-generation H1 blockers
cards.back: Cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine (astemizole and terfenadine were withdrawn for QT prolongation). Less sedating, minimal BBB penetration.

cards.front: H2 blocker with side effect of gynecomastia
H3 antagonist used for balance disorders and Meniere disease
PGE1 analog for NSAID-induced ulcers. Teratogenic effect?
cards.back: Misoprostol. Moebius sequence; also causes uterine contraction.

cards.front: PGE1 analog used to maintain PDA and treat erectile dysfunction
PGE2 analog used for cervical ripening and labor induction
PGF2-alpha analog used for postpartum hemorrhage
PGF2-alpha analog that permanently darkens iris color
PGI2 analog used for pulmonary hypertension
First-line for acute asthma per latest GINA (anti-inflammatory reliever)
cards.back: Formoterol plus inhaled corticosteroid (fast-onset long-acting beta-2 agonist)

cards.front: Quick-acting asthma reliever. Adverse effects?
cards.back: Short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, albuterol). Tremor, tachycardia.

cards.front: Drug class associated with increased asthma mortality when used alone
Methylxanthines: mechanism
cards.back: Inhibit PDE, increase cAMP, causing bronchodilation (also adenosine antagonism)

cards.front: Antidote for theophylline overdose
Drug of choice for asthma prophylaxis. Mechanism?
Advice to minimize oropharyngeal candidiasis with inhaled steroids
cards.back: Rinse the mouth and gargle after every use

cards.front: 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor and its side effects
Leukotriene receptor blockers
Mast cell stabilizers
Black box warning of montelukast
Anti-IgE antibody used in severe asthma
Mechanism of N-acetylcysteine as a mucolytic
Two major classes of antitussives
cards.back: Centrally acting (opioid, non-opioid) and peripherally acting

cards.front: Non-opioid centrally acting antitussive
Mechanism of guaifenesin (expectorant)
cards.back: Irritates gastric vagal receptors, increasing respiratory tract secretions

cards.front: Main excitatory neurotransmitters in the CNS
Main inhibitory neurotransmitters
cards.back: Brain: GABA. Spinal cord: glycine. Others: taurine, beta-alanine.

cards.front: Predominant CNS catecholamine, with a role in motivation and reward
Neurotransmitter located mostly in the ventral posterior hypothalamus for arousal, body temperature, and vascular dynamics
Neurotransmitter with roles in mood, depression, anxiety, and phobia
Uses of bupropion
Mechanism of bupropion
Features of serotonin syndrome (mnemonic FAT CHD)
cards.back: Fever, Agitation, Tremor, Clonus, Hyperreflexia, Diaphoresis

cards.front: Drug of choice for major depressive disorder
Common SSRIs
Treatment of serotonin syndrome
cards.back: Stop offending drugs, sedate with benzodiazepines, supportive care (intubate and ventilate if needed), and give cyproheptadine (5-HT2 blocker)

cards.front: Black box warning of SSRIs
cards.back: Increased risk of suicidal ideation in patients younger than 25 years

cards.front: SSRI with QT prolongation
Antidepressants with more antihistamine, alpha-blocking, and anticholinergic effects than SNRIs
Drug class that inhibits neuronal reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, with use in chronic pain
3 Cs of TCA overdose
cards.back: Coma, Convulsions, Cardiotoxicity (arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy). Treat with sodium bicarbonate.

cards.front: MAO form present in dopamine and norepinephrine neurons (brain, gut, placenta, liver)
Rapid hypertension and sympathetic symptoms when MAO inhibitors are taken with aged cheese, red wine, or pickled vegetables
Selective MAO-B inhibitors used in Parkinson disease
Black box warning of nefazodone
Drugs that can cause priapism (mnemonic: Tigas PeniS Qo, AyaW Bumaba)
cards.back: Trazodone, Papaverine, Sildenafil, Quetiapine, Alprostadil, Warfarin, Bupropion

cards.front: Adverse effects of low-potency typical antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, thioridazine): ANTI-HAM
cards.back: Antihistamine (sedation, weight gain), Antiadrenergic (hypotension, failure of ejaculation), Antimuscarinic (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation)

cards.front: Adverse effects of high-potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine)
Five black box warnings of clozapine
cards.back: 1. Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis 2. Orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, syncope 3. Seizures 4. Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy 5. Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis

cards.front: Clozapine is the drug of choice for what?
cards.back: Treatment-refractory schizophrenia and schizophrenia with suicidality

cards.front: Drugs with agranulocytosis as a serious side effect
Eye side effects of low-potency typical antipsychotics
cards.back: Chlorpromazine: corneal deposits. Thioridazine: pigmentary retinopathy.

cards.front: Antipsychotics with greater 5-HT2A than D2 affinity
Antipsychotics with the highest weight gain
Antipsychotic with high risk of sedation. Other side effects?
Antipsychotics with the highest propensity for hyperprolactinemia
Atypical antipsychotic with the lowest risk of weight gain
Antipsychotic with the lowest risk of hyperprolactinemia. Mechanism?
Drug used for acute mania and for prevention in bipolar disorder
Drugs that increase lithium levels
cards.back: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazide and other diuretics

cards.front: Teratogenic effect of lithium
cards.back: Ebstein anomaly (atrialization of the right ventricle)

cards.front: Preferred benzodiazepine as anticonvulsant maintenance
Single most effective agent for Parkinson disease
Mechanism of carbidopa
cards.back: Inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, preventing peripheral metabolism of levodopa

cards.front: COMT inhibitors
Fluctuations in motor response to levodopa. Drug of choice for off periods?
Duration of levodopa benefit becomes progressively shorter. Management?
cards.back: Wearing-off phenomenon. Add a COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor, or dopamine agonist.

cards.front: Examples of dopamine agonists
cards.back: Ergot: bromocriptine, pergolide, cabergoline. Non-ergot: pramipexole, ropinirole.

cards.front: Drugs that can cause livedo reticularis (mnemonic: A man reads FHM and GQ)
Antiviral used for parkinsonism
Anticholinergics for extrapyramidal symptoms and parkinsonism
Mechanism of benzodiazepines
cards.back: Positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A that increase the frequency of Cl- channel opening

cards.front: Benzodiazepines not metabolized by CYP (mnemonic: TOL)
Short-acting benzodiazepines (mnemonic: little TOM)
Benzodiazepines used for status epilepticus
Benzodiazepine used for alcohol withdrawal
Treatment for benzodiazepine overdose
Drug of choice for neonatal seizures
Phenobarbital derivative used for essential tremor
Barbiturate used for induction of anesthesia
Novel sedative-hypnotics used in insomnia that are faster and safer
First-line treatment for generalized anxiety disorder
cards.back: Psychotherapy with or without an SSRI (e.g., sertraline)

cards.front: Alcohol that creates toxic formate causing visual disturbance, coma, and seizures
Alcohol that creates toxic aldehydes and oxalate causing kidney damage and severe acidosis
Treatment of methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning
cards.back: Fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor). Ethanol is no longer first line.

cards.front: Mechanism of disulfiram
Antiepileptic CYP inducer with gingival hyperplasia, nystagmus, and fetal hydantoin syndrome
Antiepileptic that is a drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia. Adverse effects?
cards.back: Carbamazepine. Rash, SJS, diplopia and ataxia (most common), SIADH, megaloblastic anemia, aplastic anemia.

cards.front: Most teratogenic antiepileptic, a CYP inhibitor causing weight gain, hepatotoxicity, and pancreatitis
Black box warning of lamotrigine
cards.back: Life-threatening rash (SJS/TEN). Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis has also been reported.

cards.front: Well-tolerated AED with many anti-seizure mechanisms and weak carbonic anhydrase inhibition
cards.back: Topiramate (can cause angle closure glaucoma, kidney stones, weight loss)

cards.front: Antiepileptic associated with aplastic anemia and hepatic failure
Drug of choice for absence seizures. Mechanism?
cards.back: Ethosuximide. Reduces current through T-type calcium channels.

cards.front: AED that irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase. Major adverse effect?
Drugs of choice for postherpetic neuralgia
Mechanism of gabapentinoids
cards.back: Block alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, decreasing glutamate release

cards.front: AED that selectively binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A)
cards.back: Levetiracetam (favorable adverse effect profile, minimal drug interactions)

cards.front: Most commonly used first-line IV anesthetic
IV anesthetic reserved for patients at risk of hypotension or MI
IV anesthetic best for asthmatics and for children undergoing short, painful procedures
IV anesthetics with analgesic properties
cards.back: Ketamine (and opioids). Propofol and etomidate lack significant analgesia.

cards.front: Best measure of potency of inhaled anesthetics
cards.back: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). MAC is inversely proportional to potency (lower MAC, higher potency).

cards.front: Inhaled anesthetic with the lowest and the highest MAC
Inhaled anesthetic that can cause megaloblastic anemia and can increase ICP
Pungent inhaled anesthetics not suitable for induction or for asthmatics
Volatile anesthetic that can cause coronary steal syndrome
Non-pungent inhaled anesthetics best for asthmatics
Inhaled anesthetics with the highest propensity for reflex tachycardia
Inhaled anesthetic associated with fulminant hepatic failure
Most commonly used inhaled anesthetic in children. Nephrotoxic metabolite?
Inhaled anesthetic that lowers seizure threshold
Memory aid for ester local anesthetics
cards.back: Esters have only one 'i' in their names: tetracaine, procaine, benzocaine. Amides have two 'i's (lidocaine, bupivacaine).

cards.front: Neuromuscular blocker that undergoes Hofmann elimination yielding laudanosine (seizures)
